description: We are Niva, a team from Skopje taking on the Field Shift challenge. We are building an app that combines live readings with NASA satellite data. It helps farmers in Macedonia decide what to plant and when, compare crop rotations, save water, protect their soil and earn more from every field. Our skills: electronics, app development, data and design. Our team is complete.
summary: Niva is a web app that helps farmers in North Macedonia choose better crop rotations for their own field. Many farmers grow the same crops year after year, which wears out the soil and uses more and more water. In Niva, a farmer draws a field on a satellite map. Niva then takes 25 years of daily NASA POWER weather for that exact spot (2001 to today, over 9,400 days) and runs every candidate rotation through every one of those seasons with an FAO-56 soil-water model. It compares the rotations with what the farmer grows now: irrigation water needed, how long the soil stays covered, how much harvest is kept in dry years, and income. NASA SMAP checks the simulated soil water, MODIS NDVI shows bare-soil periods and past crops, and NASADEM/SRTM gives the slope for erosion risk. A low-cost ESP32 sensor in the field measures soil moisture, soil temperature, air temperature, humidity and pressure, and the app turns that into a live verdict and alerts. Every number links back to its data source. The app works in English and Macedonian, on a phone or a PC.
details:
Live app: https://david-zaev.github.io/niva/ (choose "Open demo", no account needed). Code and docs: https://github.com/david-zaev/niva

WHAT IT DOES

Niva answers three questions for a farmer's field:

1. What should I grow here in the next few years? At least three crop rotations are compared with what the farmer grows now, each with irrigation water needed, soil cover, dry-year harvest and income, plus the reasons, the evidence, the risks and what we don't know.

2. How is my soil doing right now? An ESP32 sensor measures soil moisture, soil temperature, air temperature, humidity and pressure and sends them over Wi-Fi (every 5 s in the demo, every 10 minutes in a real field). The app shows a verdict (Healthy / Needs attention / Poor) and live alerts, for example "Water now" when the soil holds too little plant-available water.

3. Why? Every number links back to the dataset it came from.

HOW IT WORKS

For the exact field outline, Niva downloads NASA POWER daily weather since 1 January 2001 and replays every candidate rotation through every season, day by day, with a FAO-56 soil-water balance. So the advice is not "pepper usually needs X", but "on this field, through every dry summer and wet year since 2001, this rotation needed this much water and kept this much harvest". NASA SMAP L3 Enhanced soil moisture checks that the simulated soil water rises and falls with the satellite's. MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI shows bare-soil periods and past crop patterns. NASADEM (SRTM) gives slope and erosion risk, and ISRIC SoilGrids gives soil texture, organic matter and pH. Plant-family rules make sure no crop family comes back too soon, so pests and soil diseases lose their host. We checked the engine against references: our ET0 matches the FAO-56 worked example (3.88 vs 3.9 mm/day), and our simulated root-zone water follows NASA POWER's GWETROOT over the demo farm (r = 0.62).

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Better rotations save irrigation water, keep the soil covered and healthier, and protect harvest and income in dry years. Farmers get advice for their own field instead of national averages, and the sensor turns it into day-to-day decisions.

TOOLS

Python (FastAPI, SQLite) for the API and the simulation. React and Vite with Leaflet for the web app, installable as a PWA, in English and Macedonian. ESP32 firmware (Arduino) with a capacitive soil moisture probe, a DS18B20 soil-temperature probe, a DHT22 (air temperature and humidity) and a BMP280 (air pressure). Esri World Imagery for the satellite map.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

It combines 25 years of NASA history (what usually happens on this field) with a cheap sensor in the ground (what is happening now), and explains every number in plain language for farmers.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Small family farms, rain-fed and drip-irrigated fields, a low-cost sensor, the Macedonian language, phone use in the field, and being honest about uncertainty. Niva supports farmer judgement and does not replace a local agronomist.
